t.3.2.1: Then Rāma, having been shown hospitality, at the rising of the sun took leave of all the sages and plunged deep into the forest.
t.3.2.2: A forest teeming with herds of many kinds of beasts and haunted by tigers and wolves, its trees, creepers and thickets broken down, its pools of water dreadful to behold.
t.3.2.4: But in the middle of that forest, teeming with fearsome beasts, Kākutstha saw a man-eater, huge as a mountain peak and loud of voice.
t.3.2.3: Rāma, followed by Lakṣmaṇa, beheld the middle of the forest, where the many kinds of birds had fallen silent and which resounded with swarms of crickets.
t.3.2.5: He had deep-sunken eyes and a huge mouth; he was monstrous, with a misshapen belly, loathsome, uneven of form, towering, deformed and dreadful to behold.
t.3.2.6: He was clad in a tiger's skin, moist with fat and sprinkled with blood, a terror to all beings, like Antaka, Death, with his mouth gaping wide.
t.3.2.7: Three lions, four tigers, two wolves, ten spotted deer, and the huge head of an elephant, tusks and all, smeared with fat.
t.3.2.9: Greatly enraged, he rushed forward like Kāla the Destroyer rushing upon living beings; raising a terrifying roar, he seemed to make the very earth tremble.
t.3.2.8: Having hung them upon an iron spike, he was roaring with a mighty cry. Then, seeing Rāma and Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā, the princess of Mithilā, he…
t.3.2.11: You two have entered the Daṇḍaka forest bearing arrows, bows and swords; how is it that you, who are ascetics, dwell here together with a young woman?
t.3.2.10: Taking Vaidehī up in his arms, he moved away and then said: "You two, wearing matted locks and bark garments and travelling with a wife, your lives are nearly spent."
t.3.2.13: I roam about always armed, feeding on the flesh of sages. This woman with lovely hips shall be my wife, and I shall drink the blood of you two sinful ones in battle.
t.3.2.12: Who are you two, sinful ones who practice unrighteousness and defile the sages? I am the rākṣasa named Virādha, and I roam this impassable forest.
t.3.2.14: Hearing the bold and arrogant words of the evil-minded Virādha as he spoke thus, Sītā, the daughter of Janaka, was bewildered and trembled with fear, like a plantain tree in a strong wind.
t.3.2.15: Seeing that auspicious Sītā gone into the lap of Virādha, Rāghava spoke these words to Lakṣmaṇa with a mouth that was drying up.
t.3.2.16: Look, gentle one, at my wife of virtuous conduct, the daughter born of King Janaka, the illustrious princess raised in the utmost comfort, now placed upon Virādha's lap!
t.3.2.17: Lakṣmaṇa, what Kaikeyī intended for us, what was dear to her and chosen by her boon, has quickly and fully come to pass this very day.
t.3.2.18: She who was not content with the kingdom for her son's sake, the far-sighted one by whom I, beloved of all beings, was sent away to the forest, she who is my middle mother, today at last has her desire fulfilled.
t.3.2.19: O Saumitri, nothing is more painful to me than the touch of another upon Vaidehī, not even my father's death, nor likewise the seizing of my own kingdom.
t.3.2.20: As Kākutstha spoke thus, overwhelmed with tears and grief, Lakṣmaṇa, enraged, spoke, hissing like a serpent held in check.
t.3.2.21: O Kākutstha, you are the lord of all beings and equal to Vāsava, so why do you torment yourself like one who has no protector, when you have me as your servant?
t.3.2.22: Today the earth shall surely drink the blood of the rākṣasa Virādha, struck down and lifeless by the arrow I loose in my wrath.
t.3.2.23: The anger that arose in me against Bharata, who desired the kingdom, I shall now release upon Virādha, as the wielder of the thunderbolt hurls his thunderbolt upon a mountain.
t.3.2.24: Let my mighty arrow, driven by the force and speed of my arms, fall upon his broad chest and drive the life from his body; and then let him fall, reeling, to the earth.
